ADS - Data Challenge 5: Concentration of the S&P 500 index

Omar Paviotti

2026-11-02

Assignment

Markdown

Challenge

In this data challenge, we investigate how concentrated the S&P 500 is among its constituent companies. The S&P 500 (Standard & Poor’s 500) is a stock market index that tracks the performance of 500 of the largest publicly traded companies in the United States and represents approximately 80% of the total value of the U.S. stock market. Since it is a market-capitalization-weighted index, larger companies have a substantially greater influence on its overall value and performance than smaller constituents. This makes it particularly relevant to examine how much of the index is concentrated among its largest companies.

Dataset

To obtain the dataset, we use the R package tidyquant, which integrates quantitative finance tools with the tidyverse. The package can retrieve financial data from several sources and provides access to the constituent companies of major stock market indices, including the Dow Jones Industrial Average and the S&P 500.

The constituents of the S&P 500 are retrieved using the tq_index() function. To avoid downloading the data every time the analysis is run, the dataset is saved locally as a CSV file. If the file already exists, it is loaded directly from the local directory.

dir.create("data", showWarnings = FALSE)

if (!file.exists("data/sp500.csv")) {
  sp500 <- tq_index("SP500")
  write_csv(sp500, "data/sp500.csv")
}

sp500 <- read_csv("data/sp500.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

The following interactive table provides an initial overview of the dataset.

Tidying

The dataset initially contains 505 rows, although the S&P 500 represents 500 companies. To understand this discrepancy, we first inspect two unusual observations identified by their symbols:

sp500 |>
  filter(symbol %in% c("-", "2602335D"))
## # A tibble: 2 × 8
##   symbol   company    identifier sedol  weight sector shares_held local_currency
##   <chr>    <chr>      <chr>      <chr>   <dbl> <chr>        <dbl> <chr>         
## 1 -        US DOLLAR  999USDZ92  -     5.90e-4 -       478571155. USD           
## 2 2602335D CONTRA HO… 436CVR021  -     3.00e-8 -         2578626  USD

A comparison with an independent list of S&P 500 constituents indicates that these symbols do not correspond to current components of the index. In particular, the identifier - represents the U.S. dollar rather than a company, while 2602335D is associated with a company that is no longer included in the index since April 9, 2026, following the company’s acquisition.

We therefore remove these two observations:

sp500 <- sp500 |>
  filter(symbol %notin% c("-", "2602335D"))

sp500 |>
    nrow()
## [1] 503

After their removal, the dataset contains 503 observations. However, this is actually consistent with the composition of the S&P 500: the index includes 503 common stocks issued by 500 companies because three companies are represented by two different share classes. These companies are Alphabet, Fox Corporation, and News Corp.

The corresponding stock pairs can be verified directly in the dataset:

sp500 |>
  filter(symbol %in% c(
    "GOOG", "GOOGL",
    "FOX", "FOXA",
    "NWS", "NWSA"
  )) |>
  select(symbol, company)
## # A tibble: 6 × 2
##   symbol company            
##   <chr>  <chr>              
## 1 GOOGL  ALPHABET INC CL A  
## 2 GOOG   ALPHABET INC CL C  
## 3 FOXA   FOX CORP   CLASS A 
## 4 NWSA   NEWS CORP   CLASS A
## 5 FOX    FOX CORP   CLASS B 
## 6 NWS    NEWS CORP   CLASS B

Therefore, the remaining difference between the number of observations and the number of companies is not a data error. Nevertheless, since our analysis focuses on concentration at the company level, the two share classes of each company should be combined. Their index weights are consequently added together, producing a new dataset with exactly one observation per company.

wt_sp500 <- sp500 |>
    select(symbol, company, weight) |>
    mutate(
        symbol = recode(symbol, GOOGL = "GOOG", FOXA = "FOX", NWSA = "NWS"),
        company = recode(
            symbol,
            GOOG = "ALPHABET INC",
            FOX  = "FOX CORP",
            NWS  = "NEWS CORP",
            .default = company
        )
    ) |>
    summarise(weight = sum(weight), .by = c(symbol, company)) |>
    mutate(weight = weight / sum(weight)) |>
    arrange(desc(weight))

Finally, we verify that the resulting dataset contains 500 companies and that their weights sum to one, corresponding to \(100\%\) of the index:

wt_sp500 |>
    nrow()
## [1] 500
wt_sp500 |>
    select(weight) |>
    sum()
## [1] 1

Research Questions

We will now address the research questions in order. During the analysis some overlap between them is unavoidable, since they look at the same topic, the concentration of the index weights, from different points of view.

RQ1

Research Question

How unequal are the company weights in the S&P 500?

To study the potential inequality, we start with some basic descriptive statistics: minimum, mean, standard deviation, maximum, first quartile, median and third quartile.

stats <- wt_sp500 |>
    summarise(
        Min = min(weight),
        Mean = mean(weight),
        Standard_Deviation = sd(weight),
        Max = max(weight),
        Q1 = quantile(weight, 0.25),
        Median = median(weight),
        Q3 = quantile(weight, 0.75)
    )
## # A tibble: 1 × 7
##         Min  Mean Standard_Deviation    Max       Q1   Median      Q3
##       <dbl> <dbl>              <dbl>  <dbl>    <dbl>    <dbl>   <dbl>
## 1 0.0000648 0.002            0.00649 0.0778 0.000318 0.000682 0.00141

Finally, we compute the ratio between the mean and the median.

stats$Mean / stats$Median
## [1] 2.932818

These first results already point to strong concentration. The largest weight is about 7.8%, while the smallest is almost negligible. The standard deviation (\(0.65\%\)) is more than three times the mean (\(0.2\%\)), which indicates a very high dispersion. The upper tail is also striking: the maximum is roughly 50 times the third quartile, whereas Q1 lies close to the minimum, so the distribution is compressed at the bottom and stretched at the top. Finally, the mean is about three times the median, which is a typical signature of a strongly right-skewed distribution.

We therefore proceed with a visual representation, combining in a single plot the histogram of the weights with a box plot placed on top of it.

Histogram and Box Plot Code R source code - plot_1.R Click to inspect 
hist_plot = function(wt_sp500) {
    # --- Shared x limits ---
    x_lim <- range(wt_sp500$weight)
    
    # --- Histogram ---
    hist <- wt_sp500 |>
        ggplot(aes(x = weight)) +
        geom_histogram(bins = 50, fill = "steelblue", color = "white") +
        coord_cartesian(xlim = x_lim) +
        labs(x = "Company weight (%)", y = "Number of companies")
    
    # --- Box plot ---
    box <- wt_sp500 |>
        ggplot(aes(x = weight)) +
        geom_boxplot(fill = "orange", alpha = 0.6, outlier.alpha = 0.5) +
        coord_cartesian(xlim = x_lim) +
        labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
        theme(  # Removing axis, ticks and y grid
            axis.text  = element_blank(),
            axis.ticks = element_blank(),
            panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
            panel.grid.minor.y = element_blank(),
            plot.subtitle = element_text(colour = "grey40", size=10)
        )
    
    return (
        # --- Composition ---
        box / hist +
            plot_layout(heights = c(1, 5)) +
            plot_annotation(
                title = "Distribution of S&P 500 Company Weights",
                subtitle = "The boxplot summarizes the weights, the histogram shows their frequency",
                theme = theme(plot.subtitle = element_text(colour = "grey40", size=10))
            )
    )
}

The plot confirms what the summary statistics suggested. The vast majority of companies have weights between \(0\) and \(0.01\) (\(1\%\)), and the box plot makes the compression of the bulk of the distribution very clear. Beyond that range, about ten companies stand out as extreme outliers, clearly highlighted by the box plot.

A histogram, however, only describes the shape of the distribution. To quantify the concentration of the weights, a more suitable tool is the Lorenz curve, which will be the subject of a subsequent question.

Answer

This first analysis shows that the index weights are strongly unequal: most companies have a weight below \(1\%\), while about ten of them stand out as marked outliers relative to the rest of the distribution.

RQ2

Research Question

How much of the index is represented by its largest companies?

To answer this question, we use a treemap, a visualization that divides the available area into rectangles, each with an area proportional to its value. This type of chart is often used in finance, and it gives an immediate sense of how the total is split among its components.

Tree Map Code R source code - plot_2.R Click to inspect 
tree_map <- function(wt_sp500) {
    return(
        wt_sp500 |>
            ggplot(aes(area = weight, fill = weight, label = symbol)) +
            geom_treemap(colour = "white", size = 0.5) +
            geom_treemap_text(
                aes(colour = "white"),
                place    = "centre",
                grow     = TRUE,
                padding.x = grid::unit(2.5, "mm"),
                padding.y = grid::unit(2.5, "mm")
            ) +
            scale_colour_identity() +
            scale_fill_distiller(palette = "Blues", direction = 1, trans = "sqrt") +
            labs(
                title = "Treemap of S&P 500 Company Weights",
                fill  = "Weight (%)"
            ) +
            theme(
                panel.grid = element_blank(),
                axis.text  = element_blank(),
                axis.title = element_blank(),
                axis.ticks = element_blank()
            )
    )
}

For readers who are not familiar with tickers and know companies only by name, a good alternative is a word cloud, with company names sized by weight. This requires normalizing the names of the index constituents, for example by removing redundant words such as “Inc.”, “Corp.” or “Class”. This is a task that can be effectively delegated to AI, since it does not require high precision: the goal is simply to improve the result with little effort.

Name Normalization and Word Cloud Code R source code - plot_3.R Click to inspect 
word_cloud <- function(wt_sp500) {
    
    # ---- 1. Words to remove -----------------------------------------------------
    legal <- c(
        "INC", "CORP", "CORPORATION", "CO", "COMPANY", "LTD", "LIMITED",
        "LLC", "PLC", "LP", "NV", "SA", "AG", "SE", "SPA", "NA", "DE", "THE",
        "COM", "ORD", "ADR", "SHS", "REIT", "TRUST"
    )
    
    generic <- c(
        "HOLDINGS", "HOLDING", "GROUP", "TECHNOLOGIES", "TECHNOLOGY",
        "SYSTEMS", "INTERNATIONAL", "INTL", "ENTERPRISES", "INDUSTRIES",
        "FINANCIAL", "SOLUTIONS", "PLATFORMS", "SERVICES", "WORLDWIDE",
        "GLOBAL", "BANCORP", "RESOURCES", "PARTNERS", "STORES"
    )
    
    # Manual overrides for ambiguous cases (add your own)
    overrides <- c(
        "JOHNSON & JOHNSON"  = "J&J",
        "PROCTER & GAMBLE"   = "P&G",
        "BERKSHIRE HATHAWAY" = "Berkshire",
        "JPMORGAN CHASE"     = "JPMorgan",
        "BANK OF AMERICA"    = "BofA",
        "ALPHABET"           = "Alphabet"
    )
    
    
    # ---- 2. Name-cleaning function ---------------------------------------------
    clean_name <- function(x, symbol,
                           min_len = 3, max_len = 14, short_first = 6) {
        
        s <- x %>%
            str_to_upper() %>%
            str_replace_all("\\.COM", "") %>%                           # AMAZON.COM -> AMAZON
            str_replace_all("\\b(CLASS|CL|SERIES)\\s+[A-Z]\\b", "") %>% # CLASS A, CL B
            str_replace_all("[,\\.\\(\\)\\-/']", " ") %>%
            str_squish()
        
        # Apply manual overrides to the name after removing class suffixes
        for (k in names(overrides)) {
            if (str_detect(s, paste0("^", fixed_regex(k)))) {
                return(overrides[[k]])
            }
        }
        
        w <- str_split(s, "\\s+")[[1]]
        w <- w[!w %in% c(legal, "&", "AND")]
        
        # Remove generic words, but always keep at least one word
        keep <- !w %in% generic
        if (any(keep)) w <- w[keep]
        
        if (length(w) == 0) return(symbol)
        
        # Use the first word; if it is short, append the second one
        out <- w[1]
        
        if (nchar(out) < short_first && length(w) > 1) {
            out <- paste(w[1], w[2])
        }
        
        # Formatting: keep short abbreviations uppercase,
        # otherwise use Title Case
        out <- if (!str_detect(out, " ") && nchar(out) <= 4) {
            out
        } else {
            tools::toTitleCase(str_to_lower(out))
        }
        
        out <- str_trunc(out, max_len, ellipsis = "")
        
        # Fall back to the ticker symbol if the result is too short
        if (nchar(out) < min_len) symbol else out
    }
    
    
    # Helper function to safely use override keys as regex patterns
    fixed_regex <- function(x) {
        str_replace_all(
            x,
            "([\\^\\$\\.\\|\\?\\*\\+\\(\\)\\[\\]\\{\\}\\\\&])",
            "\\\\\\1"
        )
    }
    
    
    # ---- 3. Apply the cleaning function to the data frame ----------------------
    words <- wt_sp500 |>
        mutate(
            word = map2_chr(company, symbol, clean_name),
            freq = weight * 100
        ) |>
        select(word, freq) # Word cloud requires word and freq in %
    
    # Quick check of the resulting company names
    # wt_sp500 %>%
    #     mutate(word = map2_chr(company, symbol, clean_name)) %>%
    #     select(company, word) %>%
    #     print(n = 40)
    
    # Color palette
    pal <- c(
        "#00F5D4",
        "#00BBF9",
        "#9B5DE5",
        "#F15BB5",
        "#FEE440",
        "#FF9F1C"
    )
    
    return (
        wordcloud2(
            words,
            size = 0.6,
            color = rep(pal, length.out = nrow(words)),
            backgroundColor = "#0B1020",
            minRotation = 0,
            maxRotation = 0,
            gridSize = 12
        )
    )
}

The treemap shows the concentration through area: a few large tiles take up most of the space, while the remaining companies are barely distinguishable. The word cloud shows it through text: only a handful of names are legible, and the rest, about 450 of the 500 companies, fade into the background. Both visualizations reflect the same phenomenon, namely the concentration of the index weight in a small number of companies.

The word cloud also makes it possible to identify the dominant sectors of the index. Technology comes first (Nvidia, Apple, Microsoft), followed by communication services (Alphabet, Meta) and consumer cyclical (Amazon, Tesla).

Therefore, to measure how much of the index is held by the largest companies, we can limit the analysis to the top 5 and the top 25 (\(1\%\) and \(5\%\) of the 500 companies, respectively). By simply looking at the previous representations, we can expect these to account for roughly \(25\%\) and \(50\%\) of the total weight.

wt_sp500 |>
    arrange(desc(weight)) |>
    summarise(
        Top5_WT = sum(head(weight, 5)),
        Top25_WT = sum(head(weight, 25))
    )
## # A tibble: 1 × 2
##   Top5_WT Top25_WT
##     <dbl>    <dbl>
## 1   0.295    0.527

The top 5 companies account for about \(30\%\) of the index and the top 25 for \(53\%\), so the results are in line with, and slightly above, our expectations.

Answer

The largest companies represent a very large share of the index. The top 5 companies (\(1\%\) of the 500) account for about \(30\%\) of the total weight, and the top 25 (\(5\%\)) for about \(50\%\).

RQ3

Research Question

What does the Lorenz curve tell us about concentration?

After exploring the distribution through the histogram and the treemap, we have a good idea of what to expect from the standard tool for measuring concentration: the Lorenz curve. By condensing the earlier observations into a single representation, it should offer a clearer view of how unevenly the index weight is spread across its constituents. The Lorenz curve is a graphical representation of the distribution of income or wealth. It was originally developed in 1905 to represent wealth inequality, but it is now applied in many other fields, such as ecology, economics and health.

First, the Lc function of the ineq package is used to compute the Lorenz curve, and then we build the data frame needed for plotting.

lorenz_curve <- Lc(wt_sp500$weight)

lc_df <- data.frame(p = lorenz_curve$p, L = lorenz_curve$L)

We then plot the Lorenz curve together with the line of perfect equality, highlighting the area between the two.

Lorenz Plot Code R source code - plot_4.R Click to inspect 
lorenz_plot <- function(lc_df) {
    return (
        ggplot(lc_df, aes(x = p, y = L)) +
            geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = L, ymax = p), fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.15) +  # Area
            geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey25") +  # Linear Line
            geom_line(colour = "steelblue", linewidth = 1.25) +  # Lorenz Curve
            # annotate("text", x = 0.05, y = 0.92, hjust = 0, label = paste0("Gini = ", round(gini, 3)), colour = "grey25", size = 4.5) +
            scale_x_continuous(labels = percent_format(), expand = c(0, 0)) +
            scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_format(), expand = c(0, 0)) +
            # coord_equal() +
            labs(
                title = "Lorenz Curve of S&P 500 Company Weights",
                subtitle = "The shaded area is the inequality gap, the dashed line is perfect equality",
                x = "Cumulative share of companies",
                y = "Cumulative share of weight"
            ) +
            theme(
                plot.margin = margin(10, 20, 10, 10),
                plot.subtitle = element_text(colour = "grey40", size=10)
            )
    )
}

The Lorenz curve confirms all our previous observations, with a large area separating it from the line of equality. The shares of the top \(1\%\) and top \(5\%\) seen before could be read directly from the curve, and other similar thresholds can be extrapolated visually. The area between the two curves is clearly more than half of the area under the line of equality, which suggests a high Gini coefficient.

Answer

The Lorenz curve shows a high concentration of weights in the S&P 500, confirming the evidence from the previous analysis and pointing to a high Gini coefficient.

RQ4

Research Question

What is the Gini coefficient of the S&P 500 weights?

The Gini coefficient was born as an index to accompany the Lorenz curve. It summarizes the degree of inequality in a distribution of income or wealth, and is commonly used to measure how far a distribution deviates from perfect equality. It is defined as the ratio between the area separating the line of perfect equality from the observed Lorenz curve and the area between the line of perfect equality and the line of perfect inequality. The closer the value is to 0, the closer the distribution is to perfect equality; the closer it is to 1, the more unequal the distribution.

Using the Gini() function of the ineq package, we can conclude this analysis by computing the coefficient.

Gini(wt_sp500$weight)
## [1] 0.7125411
Answer

The Gini coefficient of the S&P 500 weights is about \(0.71\), which indicates a high level of inequality. This is consistent with the whole analysis of RQ1, RQ2 and RQ3: a small number of companies carries most of the weight of the index, while the large majority contributes very little.
